title: Tesla Has a Flying Car. What Does This Mean for Archer's Flying "Taxi" Business?
detail:
Tesla Has a Flying Car. What Does This Mean for Archer's Flying "Taxi" Business?
Steven Porrello, The Motley Fool
Mon, November 2, 2026 at 3:20 PM MST 4 min read
TSLA
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

A few weeks ago, a Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) Roadster drove up a nearly vertical ramp, turned upside down, then fell -- I mean, launched itself -- into the air before its side thrusters kicked in, flipping the car upright and landing it on the road below. It was by far the most incredible maneuver I've ever seen a car pull off. The Tesla then drove out of a cloud of vapor as if nothing had happened.

If you haven't seen Tesla's new flying car, it's worth watching the video (in another stunt, the car launches itself upside down and literally barrel-rolls over five vehicles before landing upright). It's an extraordinary demonstration of engineering, and one of those rare glimpses of a future that, until recently, seemed firmly in the realm of science fiction.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

But now, what does this mean for Archer Aviation (NYSE: ACHR)? After all, Archer has also spent years developing its own flying vehicle -- an electric air taxi. If Tesla can make a flying car, will there still be a market for Archer's flying taxi, assuming it can get it certified? Let's take a look.

Image source: Archer Aviation.
Tesla's flying car is stunning, but it's not a threat to Archer

I'll just come out and say it: I don't think Tesla's flying Roadster will have an impact on Archer.

For starters, Tesla isn't really competing with Archer. Look at what Tesla is making: A sports car -- a really sleek and aesthetically striking sports car -- that can burst briefly into flight. In contrast, Archer is building an eVTOL (electric vertical takeoff and landing) vehicle that can take off and land vertically like a helicopter and transition into forward flight like a traditional airplane. It's also an engineering feat, and unlike Tesla's Roadster, it doesn't need thrusters to launch into the air.

These are obviously different vehicles, built for different purposes. And between the two, Archer's is more practical. It's designed to carry four passengers and a pilot. The Roadster, on the other hand, can only carry one person.

Archer's aircraft is also likely closer to real-world use than Tesla's. The flying Roadster might be functional, but it's not approved for road use. There's some question as to whether Tesla could ever get regulatory approval to mass-produce a flying Roadster, but even if it did, it would likely not beat Archer to the punch. Archer has already completed three of the FAA's four type-certification phases and is now working through the final one.

Rivian Automotive (NASDAQ:RIVN), an electric trucks, SUVs, and delivery vans maker, closed at $13.19, up 8.47%. UBS upgraded the stock to Buy and called the recent sell-off a buying opportunity ahead of the R2 ramp. Investors are watching early R2 demand and margin progress next.

Trading volume reached 64.3 million shares, coming in about 165% above its three-month average of 24.3 million shares. Rivian Automotive IPO'd in 2021 and has fallen 87% since going public.

How the markets moved today

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) fell 0.50% to 7,542, while the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) dropped 1.07% to 25,164. Among electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing, passenger EVs, and commercial delivery vans peers, Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) closed at $403.82, up 1.00%, and Ford Motor (NYSE:F) finished at $12.60, up 2.86%, as EV-capable automaker stocks moved higher on strong recent quarterly results.

What this means for investors

On Monday, Nov. 2, UBS upgraded Rivian Automotive to Buy from Neutral/Hold and kept its $17 target, saying the sell-off was overdone ahead of the company's R2 ramp. UBS also said early R2 demand looks solid and expects Rivian to exit 2026 with a positive automotive gross margin percentage. That margin path is central to the stock's rerating.

Rivian's third-quarter results showed revenue up 38% year over year to $2.2 billion, with gross profit of $176 million, an increase of $152 million over the prior year. The company's budget R2 vehicle became its best selling auto by volume in Q3, demonstrating consumer demand for the all-electric midsize SUV is strong. The report gave the stock a fresh fundamental backdrop before the UBS call.

Rivian also said its Volkswagen joint venture received a $1 billion term loan in October. That financing adds liquidity context as the company works through its R2 launch.

So far, Rivian looks like it's on a growth trajectory despite a volatile macroeconomic environment of rising interest rates, thanks to its R2 release. This is quite an achievement, especially after federal EV subsidies were ended in 2025. The UBS upgrade further validates Rivian's strategic bet on R2 is a win.

title: Musk warned America will go 1,000% bankrupt. Now U.S. debt tops $40 trillion and counting
detail:
Musk warned America will go 1,000% bankrupt. Now U.S. debt tops $40 trillion and counting
Bibhu Pattnaik
Mon, November 2, 2026 at 3:15 PM MST 4 min read
SPCX
TSLA
BTC-USD
Trade SPCX on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Elon Musk's two biggest companies are sitting on 30,221 Bitcoin. At Bitcoin's Oct. 31 close of $77,424, those coins are worth about $2.34 billion. SpaceX owns more than 60% of them.

The rocket maker disclosed 18,712 BTC in its IPO filing, bought for about $661 million, or roughly $35,000 a coin. That stake is now worth about $1.45 billion, more than double its cost.

Related: Elon Musk warns America will 1,000% go bankrupt and fail as a country

Tesla holds the other 11,509 BTC, worth about $891 million.Those coins carry new weight as the U.S. debt clock pushes past $40.6 trillion, a number Musk has spent the year calling a path to national bankruptcy.

Musk's crypto ties run beyond his own balance sheets.

When he mocked Binance after its record $6.3 billion hack last week, co-founder Changpeng Zhao reminded him that the exchange's $500 million bet on his Twitter takeover is now worth more than $1 billion in SpaceX shares.

Musk's case for America's bankruptcy

In a February podcast where he warned the U.S. is heading for bankruptcy.

"We are 1000% going to go bankrupt as a country and fail as a country without AI and robots," Musk said on the Dwarkesh Podcast in February this year. "Nothing else will solve the national debt."

Nine months later, the U.S. national debt stands at about $40.6 trillion, according to the latest information from Peter G. Peterson Foundation's debt clock, which tracks Treasury data.

That works out to $118,939 for every person in the country. Interest alone costs the government more than $2.8 billion a day, and the foundation projects it will nearly double within a decade.

Borrowing costs are rising too. The 30-year Treasury yield climbed above 5.7% in early October, its highest since 2002, while the 10-year topped 5.3%.

Musk led President Donald Trump's DOGE cost-cutting effort for about four months in 2025. He now says that experience proved spending cuts won't get there.

"The only way we're going to solve the national debt is with AI and robots," Musk told biographer Walter Isaacson in an interview that premiered Oct. 20. "We're not gonna solve it by trying to save our way there."

He also admitted he "got carried away" during his time in Washington.

Related: Dave Ramsey's investing advice falls short, study finds

Why Bitcoin bulls are watching

Bitcoin's capped supply of 21 million coins has made it a popular pitch as a hedge against runaway government debt and money printing.

Musk has made that argument himself. "Bitcoin is based on energy: you can issue fake fiat currency, and every government in history has done so, but it is impossible to fake energy," he wrote on X in October 2025.

title: Elon Musk sends incredible news to Micron stock investors
detail:
Elon Musk sends incredible news to Micron stock investors
Hillary Remy, Celine Provini
Mon, November 2, 2026 at 2:23 PM MST 6 min read
MU
TSLA
SPCX
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

One post from Elon Musk was enough to jolt Micron Technology stock.

The Tesla and SpaceX CEO replied on X to an analyst at Citrini Research, a firm that offers thematic equity and macro trading insights. Musk noted that the amount of memory humanoid robots need "will exceed everything else on Earth."

Micron shares rose about 2.5% after the remark.

The timing could hardly be better for the memory maker. Micron fell about 6% on Oct. 22 as another AI sell-off hit chip stocks, the same day the company held a technology webinar for analysts.

Musk's comment gave bulls a new story to tell, and this one has nothing to do with data centers. It is about machines that walk, lift, and work alongside people.

Robots could become memory's next big customer

Musk made the remark on Oct. 26, in a post that quickly spread across investor circles.

His post listed the robot chip's memory as LP5, a low-power type of DRAM that also goes into phones and laptops, Benzinga reported. The robot memory story still assumes builders can actually get the chips they need.

Also read: Nvidia and Micron are about to lord their successes all over Wall Street

Research firms see a big runway. Counterpoint Research expects DRAM demand from humanoids to climb more than 20 times between 2026 and 2030, with memory in each robot rising from about 19GB today to 39GB by the end of the decade, according to The Motley Fool.

That would add a fresh source of demand on top of data centers, smartphones, vehicles, and personal computers.

Musk thinks that may still be too low. In early October, he said in X that Tesla halved the memory on its AI5 chip to 72GB and cut the AI6 chip by a third to 144GB, calling it "the only way to get enough volume for Optimus production."

He added that the cuts should have a negligible effect on performance, since memory bandwidth matters more than total capacity. Even after the cuts, both chips carry far more memory than Counterpoint's per-robot estimate.

The cuts also showed how tight supply has become. JPMorgan said the memory shortage is lasting longer than analysts expected, and Micron's management believes DRAM and NAND markets will stay tight beyond 2027.

Citi raised its own target to $1,300, citing stronger DRAM pricing and continued undersupply, TheStreet reported.

Tesla and Toyota are building toward scale

Tesla is moving from talk to production. The company has started early production of Optimus at its Fremont, California, factory and targets initial customer shipments towards the end of 2027, with Musk saying delivery is likely toward the end of next year.

title: North Korea's Bitcoin heist is worth 3x its exports and more than Tesla holds
detail:
North Korea's Bitcoin heist is worth 3x its exports and more than Tesla holds
Bibhu Pattnaik
Mon, November 2, 2026 at 1:00 PM MST 3 min read
BTC-USD
TSLA
Trade BTC on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

North Korea's hackers have walked away from the Binance heist with a Bitcoin pile that most corporate treasuries can't match.

The FBI on Oct. 31 formally blamed North Korea for the theft of more than $6 billion from Binance, naming the state-backed hacking group it tracks as TraderTraitor.

The TRM Labs puts total losses at about $6.36 billion across ten blockchains. Of that, 18,270 BTC was sent to a single address and then split across 19 wallets.

The FBI had published a list of cryptocurrency addresses linked to the attack and urged anyone with relevant information to contact a local FBI field office or submit a report through its Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.gov.

TraderTraitor was not a new designation for the bureau. The FBI had also used the same name in February 2025, when it attributed the $1.5 billion Bybit hack to North Korea.

Related: Elon Musk has a bold answer to America's $40 trillion debt crisis

Bigger than Tesla, El Salvador and Pyongyang's trade

At about $78,500 per coin, the stolen Bitcoin is worth roughly around $1.4 billion.

That is nearly three times North Korea's total merchandise exports last year, which the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency put at $468.59 million, a North-Korean daily reported.

The haul is also about 59% larger than Tesla's 11,509 BTC, and it sits just 442 coins short of SpaceX's 18,712 BTC.

The figure is 2.3 times the approximately 7,820 Bitcoin held in the reserve wallet disclosed by El Salvador's National Bitcoin Office.

The Central American country began accumulating Bitcoin in September 2021 under President Nayib Bukele, making it the first nation to adopt the cryptocurrency as legal tender.

Popular on TheStreet Roundtable

Binance major shareholder cites $1B SpaceX stake after Elon Musk mocks hack

I'm with Elon Musk on Binance's hack

Binance says 90% of hack impact now covered

Why Bitcoin is the hardest part to claw back

About $3 billion of the stolen assets has been frozen so far, most of it stablecoins. Tether locked about $1.77 billion and Circle about $825 million.

Bitcoin has no issuer that can block a wallet. It can only be stopped once it hits an exchange or custodian, Seoul Economic Daily noted. The FBI has published the 19 Bitcoin addresses and urged service providers to block transactions with them.

"A freeze stops the money from moving, and recovery follows through legal process," Ari Redbord of TRM Labs told CNBC.

The market took the hit in stride. Bitcoin slid about 5%, from roughly $80,769 before the theft to near $76,400 by Friday afternoon.

Worries over how the AI data center buildout gets paid for are back in focus. Applied Digital (NASDAQ:APLD) stock is at $16.33 in afternoon trading, down 8%. The drop follows comments from CEO Wes Cummins, who stated the company still needs to finance about 800 megawatts (MW) of data center capacity over the next 12 months.

shironosov / iStock

Over the past year, Applied Digital stock is down 51%. AI cloud and data center peers are slipping alongside it, a sign the market reads a funding gap at one builder as a question for the whole group.

Applied Digital's CEO Lays Out the Funding Gap

In his November 2 interview, Wes Cummins said Applied Digital has financed about 600 MW of its 1.4-gigawatt (GW) plan. He rejected the "neocloud" label, stating, "We're effectively a highly technical real estate business. Long-term leases, high-quality tenants."

Cummins maintained bank construction loans, project financing and the bond market remain open to Applied Digital, though higher Treasury yields and wider credit spreads have raised borrowing costs. The CEO said the capacity still awaiting financing has tenants rated AA or better. Applied Digital also cited about $20 billion of contracted revenue at its three newer campuses.
